We thank the reviewer for their time and feedback.
We incorporated most of their feedback, strengthening our paper.
Below we answer their questions and hope that the reviewer considers raising their score if there are no further concerns.

>The main theoretical result is for the deterministic case. Can you please elaborate and provide the reader confidence that the stochastic version (which was implemented) converges or finds a good solution? Can the existing analysis be extended to the stochastic setting, perhaps under certain assumptions about variance reduction?

Thanks for pointing out this shortcoming. 
In the mean time we **extended our convergence analysis** to the case where the algorithm uses **stochastic gradients for the lower level problem**.
We **added the new result** to the manuscript.
Extending this to the higher level problem is currently out of reach unless one is willing to impose convexity assumptions as in the original LinBreg work or indeed use variance reduction.
Even for standard (one level) mirror descent a stochastic convergence analysis without convexity and variance reduction is notoriously difficult and seems to be unavailable.
We explained this in the updated version of the paper.

We further provide a convergence analysis for the setting in which the loss admits a finite-sum structure. By incorporating a linear correction term into the coarse objective, we relate the resulting multilevel scheme to variance-reduction methods and thereby establish its convergence, see Appendix B of the revised manuscript.

>The theoretical FLOPs claims are strong. Could you please provide any practical wall-clock time results [...] to demonstrate whether these theoretical savings translate to real-world speedups?

We completely agree. This was also pointed out by other reviewers. 
We do acknowledge that theoretical FLOP counts do not directly translate to wall-clock time savings and the latter would require sparsity-aware implementations of forward and backward passes.
The reason why we reported FLOPs was to use the same metric as other papers, e.g., the seminal one on "rigging the lottery'' (Evci et al., 2020).

To investigate potential time savings we added an experiment on CIFAR10, wherein we train ResNet18 for 10 epochs using implementations of convolutional and linear layers that exploit unstructured sparsity, only available on CPU. 
We achieved a **training time reduction of 49%** compared to the PyTorch implementation (see Figure 2).

We did record training times for the considered problems on our GPU cluster but found it impossible to report consistent results -- even when using the same seed. 
We suspect the presence of other jobs and similar overhead at the cluster pollute our time measurements.

>Could you please provide a more detailed derivation for the LinBreg baseline's FLOPs cost ($2f_S + f_D$)? Specifically, how is a full, dense gradient $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(k)})$ computed at a cost that is not at least $f_D$ (forward) + $2f_D$ (backward) = $3f_D$?

For the computation of theoretical FLOPs, we followed the paper on ``rigging the lottery'' (Evci et al., 2020) for comparability. 
They argue, that for a sparse network the forward pass and back-propagating the error need $2\cdot f_S$ FLOPs and for the dense gradients that need to be computed another $f_D$ FLOPs are necessary, leading to $2\cdot f_S + f_D$ in total. 
The theoretical FLOPs for LinBreg align with those for SNFS, since both methods require dense gradients, while the theoretical FLOPs for our method align with RigL, where the dense gradients are only required every $m$-th iteration.

>The choice of m=99 seems to be a fixed, simplifying assumption. How sensitive is the final model's accuracy to this choice? Could a smaller m (e.g., m=10) with a different $\lambda$ achieve a similar result? A 2D-ablation plot showing final accuracy/sparsity for different pairs of (m, $\lambda$) would greatly improve the paper's practical utility. (Please point me to the explanation if I missed it in Appendix)

We would like to refer to Figure 4 in our revised paper (Figure 2 in the original paper) which actually provides such an ablation study for a subset of the parameter space. 
We investigate the effect of $\lambda$ for fixed $m$ and the effect of $m$ for fixed $\lambda$.
Besides the usual sparsity-accuracy trade-off we can observe that already very small regularization strength suffices to achieve very good sparsity.
Furthermore, the sensitivity with respect to the switching frequency seems rather modest and affects sparsity much more than it affects accuracy.
Overall, a small regularization combined with modest to slow switching frequency appears to be the best choice.

While a full search over a rectangle in parameter space would probably shed even more light on these effects, we are lacking the compute to perform such an experiment (which would require $100$ training runs / $1,000$ GPU hours) in a reasonable amount of time.

summary.value: The paper proposes a dynamic sparse training algorithm that combines linearized Bregman iterations with periodic freezing of the network structure. Training alternates between full updates and phases where only currently nonzero parameters are updated, which exploits emerging sparsity while exploring the sparse parameter space.

strengths.value:
+Clear optimizer view that unifies sparse training with mirror descent and Bregman iterations, including explicit proximal updates and a principled route to sparsity.

+Multilevel design that freezes structure and updates only active parameters, with formal handling of restriction and prolongation and a stated convergence result.

+Theoretical FLOP reductions relative to standard Bregman iterations are articulated and support the motivation for the freezing schedule.

weaknesses.value:
-Convergence relies on relative smoothness and a PL-type inequality and is stated for exact gradients, so the guarantees do not directly cover the stochastic setting used in practice.
-The paper discusses potential computational savings but does not provide wall clock training speedups, energy, or memory profiles on hardware.
-The current evaluation focuses only on small-image vision classification tasks, which limits the generality of the findings. Such experiments may not capture the behavior of the proposed sparse training method on larger-scale datasets or different architectures like transformers.
-Recent related works [1][2][3][4][5][6][7] should be compared and discussed.
[1] Sparse Training via Boosting Pruning Plasticity with Neuroregeneration, NeurIPS 2021
[2] Top-kast: Top-k always sparse training NeurIPS 2020
[3] AC/DC: Alternating Compressed/DeCompressed Training of Deep Neural Networks, NeurIPS 2021
[4] Dynamic Sparsity Is Channel-Level Sparsity Learner, NeurIPS 2023
[5] Advancing Dynamic Sparse Training by Exploring Optimization Opportunities, ICML 2024
[6] NeurRev: Train Better Sparse Neural Network Practically via Neuron Revitalization, ICLR 2024
[7] A Single-Step, Sharpness-Aware Minimization is All You Need to Achieve Efficient and Accurate Sparse Training, NeurIPS 2024

summary.value: The paper propose a DST algorithm, "Multilevel LinBreg" (ML LinBreg), which is based on linearized Bregman iterations (or mirror descent). The key novelty of the method is to alternate between two phases: a "fix" phase, where the network's sparsity pattern is frozen (only non-zero weights are trained), and a "explore" phase, where a single, full-level mirror descent step is taken, allowing the sparsity pattern to evolve. This fix-and-explore cycle is designed to drastically reduce computational costs, as the expensive, full-gradient "explore" step is performed only for a portion of the training time. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate that ML LinBreg can produce models that are sparser and more accurate than the standard LinBreg algorithm.

strengths.value:
1) The core idea of alternating between a "fix" sparse-training phase (the m coarse steps) and a "explore" phase (the 1 fine step) is simple, elegant, and well-motivated.

2) The paper's primary selling point is the massive theoretical reduction in FLOPs as shown in Appendix B. The authors demonstrate the source of the savings: standard LinBreg must compute a dense gradient at every step, while ML LinBreg only does so 1 out of every m+1 steps.

3) The proposed ML LinBreg consistently outperforms its most logical baseline, standard LinBreg, by achieving better accuracy at similar sparsity levels, or higher sparsity at similar accuracy. Furthermore, it demonstrates competitive or superior performance compared to a standard prune-and-fine-tune (PFT) baseline, without the need to first train a dense model.

4)By embedding the algorithm into a multilevel optimization framework, the authors connect it to a rich body of existing literature.

weaknesses.value:
1) I think the paper can be made better by explaining the mismatch between the theoretical analysis and the practical implementation. The convergence guarantee (Theorem 1) is provided for the deterministic (exact gradient) setting. However, the algorithm is implemented using mini-batch "unbiased estimators" (Algorithm 1), which is a stochastic setting.

2) The headline-grabbing FLOPs reduction (to 6%) is entirely theoretical. This calculation assumes that unstructured sparsity (e.g., from $l_1$ shrinkage) translates directly to a proportional decrease in wall-clock time. This is notoriously false on modern hardware like GPUs, which are optimized for dense, contiguous matrix operations.

3) The FLOPs calculation for the baseline LinBreg method ($2f_S + f_D$ in Appendix B) is confusing and inadequately explained. The update rule for LinBreg (Eq. 4a) requires the full gradient $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(k)})$, which is dense. It is not clear how this can be computed with a sparse forward pass ($f_S$) and a single dense term ($f_D$). A dense gradient typically requires a dense backward pass, which itself is often preceded by a dense forward pass. The paper needs to be much clearer on the assumptions that lead to the $2f_S + f_D$ formula, as the entire 38% vs. 6% comparison hinges on it.

summary.value: The goal of the work is to improve efficient training of deep neural networks. To this end it proposes to use mirror descent to train sparse neural networks combined with switching between coarse and fine phases to reduce the amount of updates needed. The pruning is done with soft thresholding. The method proposed is ML LinBreg or Multilevel LinBreg and is evaluated on standard vision benchmarks against another mirror (Bregman) based method LinBreg and standard pruning. The method is competitive or performs better then LinBreg.

strengths.value: The work is well motivated by the goal of improving efficiency of training. The combination of switching between regimes is interesting in the context of mirror descent applied to sparsity. This can combine the benefits of dynamics sparse training methods like RiGL with geometric optimization principles. Providing theory for convergence could help formalize sparse training algorithms. The empirical evaluation on standard vision benchmarks further supports the utility of the approach.

weaknesses.value:
The main weakness of this work is that it does not compare with related baselines in sparse training such as RiGL.
Moreover, the current experiments are of small scale, extending the experiments to ResNet50 on ImageNet for example would make it also easier to compare with other methods. 


Another limitation is the limited discussion of the literature on pruning and sparse training. Some works that seem to be relevant based on type of algorithm proposed:

Sparse training strategy based on proximal formulation:

[1] Kusupati, Aditya et al. “Soft Threshold Weight Reparameterization for Learnable Sparsity.” International Conference on Machine Learning (2020).


Mirror flow formulation:

[2] Jacobs, Tom and Rebekka Burkholz. “Mask in the Mirror: Implicit Sparsification.” ArXiv abs/2408.09966 (2024): n. pag.


Alternating between dense and sparse phase:

[3] Peste, Alexandra et al. “AC/DC: Alternating Compressed/DeCompressed Training of Deep Neural Networks.” Neural Information Processing Systems (2021).


Using Fisher information:

[4] Singh, Sidak Pal and Dan Alistarh. “WoodFisher: Efficient second-order approximations for model compression.” ArXiv abs/2004.14340 (2020): n. pag.

To summarize, this work proposes an interesting modification of LinBreg for sparse training, however the limited comparison with other methods and scale of the experiments limits relevancy of the work. Given this I would vote for marginally reject.

We thank the reviewer for their time and feedback. We incorporated a lot of their feedback, strengthening our paper. Below we answer their questions and hope that the reviewer considers raising their score if there are no further concerns.

>The main weakness of this work is that it does not compare with related baselines in sparse training such as RiGL.

This is a valid and important point. We are currently extending our experiments by incorporating RigL for the considered datasets and architectures. Since our considered model architecture is different to ones used in their original paper, we need to ensure we use the best hyperparameters for RigL as to not misrepresent it. We will include the corresponding results as soon as they become available.

>Moreover, the current experiments are of small scale, extending the experiments to ResNet50 on ImageNet for example would make it also easier to compare with other methods.

Thanks for pointing this out. We completely agree that evaluations on larger image data sets or other architectures would further demonstrate generality of our method. Unfortunately, we are lacking the computational resources to extend the exhaustive experimental studies, e.g., Figures 1 and 3, to such settings. Each such figure requires an extra $~100$ entire training runs which we project to require (for ImageNet with ResNet50) approx. 2,000 GPU hours.

Note that we did add a new experiment to investigate potential time savings wherein we train ResNet18 for 10 epochs using implementations of convolutional and linear layers that exploit unstructured sparsity, but only available on the CPU. This leads to a **training time reduction of 49%** compared to the PyTorch implementation.

>Another limitation is the limited discussion of the literature on pruning and sparse training. [...]

Thanks for pointing us to these references which slipped our attention. We incorporated them into our discussion.

>Can the experimental results be improved by training less long in the coarse regime? (If possible plot this on a curve)

This is very valid question and we would like to refer to Figure 4(b) of the revised paper (Figure 2(b) of the original submission) and the short discussion thereafter to answer it: As expected, by training less long in the coarse regime the resulting accuracy can be slightly improved at the cost of losing a lot of sparsity. At the same time, the plot also shows that the loss of accuracy is only very mild when training longer in the coarse regime. Therefore, we identified medium long coarse regimes (corresponding to $m\approx 20-100$) as best in terms of balancing accuracy and sparsity. We have also changed the caption associated with the figure to highlight its exploration of $m.$

>Another consideration for this type of algorithm is the effect hyperparameters such as weight decay and learning rate can this be ablated and expanded upon in the appendix on CIFAR10, ResNet18 for example?

We agree that, as with any optimization algorithm the precise hyperparameter configuration can lead to different performance and, in this context, sparsity of the model. 
A key benefit of our algorithm is that we do not need explicit weight decay in our training loss, rather, the analogue of weight decay is the regularizer in the proximal step, whose potency is controlled by $\lambda.$ We explore the effects of varying the value of $\lambda$ in Figure 4. 

We decided upon our initial learning rate and learning rate schedule based upon similar experiments in other papers. 
We promise to include an ablation study regarding the learning rate in the Appendix for the final paper.

We would like to thank all reviewers for the valuable time and feedback. 
Here we summarize the main changes of our paper.
We believe that the reviewers' comments helped us to strengthen our paper significantly.

**Summary of the reviews**

*Pros:* Reviewers highlighted that our method is well-motivated by the goal of making training more efficient, outperforms SGD and other sparse training baselines in terms of theoretical FLOPs, and is complemented by a rigorous convergence analysis.

*Cons:* Reviewers asked for a more general convergence analysis allowing for stochastic gradients, further experiments on large scale datasets and architectures, as well as wall clock time measurements that demonstrate the efficacy of our method.

We provided point-to-point replies for all the points raised by the reviewers. Here we sum up the most important changes we made to our paper.

**Important changes**
1. We extended our convergence analysis to the case of using stochastic gradients on the coarse problem (which is where most iterations take place).
2. We added an experiment which shows that using sparse implementations of forward and backward passes on CPUs (SparseProp) we achieve a training time reduction of 49%. This complements the savings in terms of theoretical FLOPs of our method.
3. We added missing relevant papers to our literature review and are currently running comparisons with RigL.

title.value: Summary of the Rebuttal for the AC

comment.value:
Dear AC,

We would like to provide a concise summary of the review discussion and of the substantial improvements made during the rebuttal period, to facilitate your assessment.

**Overall reviewer consensus.**  
All reviewers found the method well-motivated and the multilevel formulation conceptually appealing. They appreciated the clear optimizer-based view, the rigorous convergence analysis, and the strong empirical sparsity–accuracy trade-offs compared to LinBreg and pruning baselines. Concerns centered on (1) extending the theory to the stochastic setting, (2) providing practical computational evidence beyond theoretical FLOPs, (3) comparing to recent DST baselines such as RigL, (4) clarifying hyperparameter sensitivity, and (5) literature coverage.

Before the discussion period ended early, reviewer Cs66 expressed their willingness to raise their score based on (3) and (4) which, in our opinion, turned out favorable for the proposed method.

**Key issues raised and how we addressed them.**

1. **Convergence analysis in the stochastic setting.**  
   We significantly extended the theoretical part of the paper. The updated manuscript now includes a convergence result (Theorem 1) for the practically relevant case where stochastic gradients are used on the coarse (lower-level) problem. We also added a finite-sum analysis showing how a linear correction term connects our multilevel approach to variance-reduction methods (Theorem 2). 

2. **Practical computational benefits.**  
   Reviewers requested empirical speedups in addition to theoretical FLOPs. We added a new CIFAR-10 experiment using sparsity-aware CPU implementations of convolutional and linear layers (SparseProp). This demonstrates a **49\% reduction in wall-clock training time** (Figure 2), supporting the claim that ML LinBreg can translate theoretical savings into real efficiency when sparse kernels are available. GPU timing on our shared cluster was too noisy to be reliable, which we report transparently.

3. **Comparison with modern DST baselines (RigL).**  
   We implemented RigL and added the results to Figure 1 for a direct comparison. **ML LinBreg consistently matches RigL accuracy and shows markedly higher robustness across common mask-initialization schemes** (uniform, Erdős–Rényi, and ER-kernel), see Table  2 in Appendix D. This directly addresses the main missing-baseline concern from multiple reviewers.

4. **Hyperparameter sensitivity and guidance.**  
   We expanded the discussion around Figure 4 to clarify how sparsity and accuracy vary with:
   
   - the coarse/fine switching frequency $m$,
   
   - the regularization parameter $\lambda$.
   
   We find that accuracy is robust to $m$, while sparsity varies more strongly, and that modest-to-slow switching frequencies ($\approx 50-100$ coarse iterations per fine one) with small regularization offer the best balance. Since reviewers requested large-scale guidance, we added Figure 7 on a larger scale setting which exhibits similar behavior. 
   
5. **Literature coverage and citation corrections.**  
   We substantially updated the related-work section, adding missing pruning, dynamic sparsity, mirror-descent, and proximal-formulation references, and corrected several citation inaccuracies pointed out during discussion.

**Summary of strengths after revision.**

- A principled multilevel sparse training method grounded in mirror descent / Bregman iterations.  

- New stochastic convergence results and finite-sum/variance-reduction interpretation not present in the initial submission.  

- Demonstrated practical speedup (49\%) using existing sparse backpropagation implementations.  

- Strong, robust empirical performance, including new comparisons showing higher reliability than RigL under multiple initialization schemes.  

- Clearer ablations and hyperparameter guidance, plus expanded related work.

We hope this summary helps clarify the current state of the paper and how the reviewers’ main concerns have been addressed.  
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,  
The Authors

summary.value: Reviewers generally viewed the paper as a well-motivated optimization-based approach to dynamic sparse training, with a clear formulation grounded in multilevel mirror descent and encouraging empirical results on standard vision benchmarks. At the same time, several concerns were raised regarding the gap between theory and practice, particularly the reliance on deterministic analysis versus stochastic mini-batch training. Reviewers also questioned whether the proposed method yields practical wall-clock efficiency gains, noted insufficient comparisons to strong and contemporary dynamic sparse training baselines, and asked for clearer guidance on hyperparameter sensitivity and broader empirical validation.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The rebuttal partially addresses several of the main concerns by extending the discussion toward stochastic optimization, expanding and correcting the related-work section, providing additional empirical results and guidance on hyperparameter sensitivity, and adding a missing baseline. In particular, a comparison with RigL was added in response to reviewer requests, which partially helps clarify the relationship to prior dynamic sparse training methods.

However, several concerns remain only partially resolved. The RigL comparison is limited to a small-scale setting, and RigL represents a relatively mature baseline; as a result, questions about relative efficiency and accuracy, particularly in comparison to stronger or more recent dynamic sparse training methods under realistic training regimes, remain open. While the paper does not demonstrate end-to-end wall-clock speedups on standard GPU training pipelines, this limitation is largely orthogonal to the paper’s main algorithmic contribution and reflects a broader, community-wide challenge in effectively exploiting sparsity during training. Broader validation beyond small-scale vision benchmarks also remains an open question

reviewer_scores.value: While it is difficult to precisely estimate how individual reviewers would have updated their scores given the limited discussion, it is likely that most scores would remain in a similar range, without a clear consensus shift, as the rebuttal primarily improves completeness and interpretation rather than introducing fundamentally new empirical evidence. There is no clear indication that scores would have decreased. Overall, the paper appears promising, but would likely benefit from further empirical and theoretical strengthening, as reflected in the reviewer feedback.

>Offers a convergence proof adapting results from ML-BPGD and relative smoothness theory

In the revised version of our manuscript we further **extended our convergence analysis** to using **stochastic gradients for the lower level problem**.
    
We additionally provide a convergence analysis for the case in which the loss has a finite-sum structure, showing that by incorporating a linear correction term into the coarse objective, the resulting algorithm can be related to variance-reduction methods. This analysis can be found in Appendix B of the revised manuscript.

>Limited to small-scale image datasets, lacks evaluation on large-scale or transformer architectures to demonstrate generality.  

Thanks for pointing this out.

Each such Figure would require an extra $~100$ entire training runs which we project to require (for ImageNet with ResNet50) approx. 2,000 GPU hours.

>FLOP analysis is theoretical. It would be good to have experimental results.

We completely agree and we acknowledge that theoretical FLOPs do not directly translate to computational savings.
In the first version of our manuscript we claimed that our method only reduces the "theoretical number of FLOPs'' and has the "potential to substantially reduce training time and resource requirements''.
We toned down this last statement and some other statements in the conclusion to better align with the fact that, as is common for other sparse training papers, computational savings are primarily theoretical. 
Indeed, the reason we reported FLOPs was to use the same metric as said papers, e.g., the seminal one on "rigging the lottery'' (Evci et al., 2020).

Still, to support the claim that our method has the potential for computational savings we have included an additional CIFAR10 experiment wherein we train ResNet18 for 10 epochs using implementations of convolutional and linear layers that exploit unstructured sparsity, but are only available on the CPU. 
This leads to a **training time reduction of 49\%** compared to the PyTorch implementation (see Figure 2).

>Missing recent dynamic sparse training baselines and structured-pruning comparisons.

We acknowledge that the literature is this field is expanding very rapidly and we missed to discuss some recent methods. 
This was also pointed out by other reviewers and we incorporated and discussed the methods they suggested.
We are currently running experiments for existing sparse training baselines, such as RigL, and will include their performance for some of the sparsity levels attained by the already-included algorithms. 
Since our considered model architecture is different to ones used in their original paper, we need to ensure we use the best hyperparameters for RigL as to not misrepresent it.

>Could the authors report actual training time and energy savings to complement the theoretical FLOP reduction?

As mentioned in our answer above, it is common for current implementations of sparse training algorithms to calculate full gradients and only mimic sparse training by applying a mask.
We highlight this discrepancy between theory and implementations in the discussion around our new CIFAR10 experiment, which demonstrates a training time reduction of 49% when employing sparse implementations of convolutional and linear layers on CPU. 


We did record training times for the considered problems on our GPU cluster but found it impossible to report consistent results -- even when using the same seed. 
We suspect the presence of other jobs and similar overhead at the cluster pollute our time measurements.

>How sensitive is convergence to the switching frequency and the choice of regularizer?

We would like to refer to our ablation study in Figure 4 of the updated manuscript (Figure 2 of the original submission) where we investigated the effect of the regularization strength for fixed switching frequency and, vice versa, the effect of the switching frequency for fixed regularization.
Besides the usual sparsity-accuracy trade-off we can observe that already very small regularization strength suffices to achieve very good sparsity.
Furthermore, the sensitivity of accuracy with respect to the switching frequency seems rather modest, whereas sparsity is affected much more.
Hence, a small regularization combined with modest to slow switching frequency of $m\approx 20-100$ appears to be the best choice.

summary.value: This paper proposes Multilevel LinBreg, a sparse training algorithm derived from linearized Bregman iterations combined with multilevel optimization. The method alternates between fine and coarse updates. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet show that the method achieves higher sparsity and comparable or better accuracy than LinBreg and pruning baselines, while theoretically reducing FLOPs to as low as 6% of SGD training.

strengths.value:
1. Offers a convergence proof adapting results from ML-BPGD and relative smoothness theory
2. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet (ResNet-18, VGG-16, WideResNet-28-10) consistently support claims of sparsity and efficiency.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited to small-scale image datasets, lacks evaluation on large-scale or transformer architectures to demonstrate generality.
2. FLOP analysis is theoretical. It would be good to have experimental results.
3. Missing recent dynamic sparse training baselines and structured-pruning comparisons.

2. How sensitive is convergence to the switching frequency and the choice of regularizer?

>How should the coarse update frequency and the restriction criterion be selected in practice, and how sensitive are results to these hyperparameters?

Regarding the choice of the coarse update frequency (m=99) we refer to our ablation study in Figure 4(b) of the revised paper.
In fact, accuracy is much less affected by its choice than sparsity.
Hence, choosing a medium to slow frequency of one fine update after around 50-100 coarse ones, seems to give the best results without sacrificing too much accuracy.

Furthermore, we have run some comparisons with RigL for training a ResNet18 model on CIFAR10. 
In summary, **our method is far more robust to the initialization of the model**, in particular, that of the sparse mask. 
We consider uniform, Erdős–Rényi  and Erdős–Rényi-kernel mask initialization schemes and perform the variance-preserving rescaling of the non-masked weights as mentioned in our manuscript (we also divide this rescaling factor by 2 as this leads to slightly better results). 
We compare the performance of ML LinBreg and RigL with a target sparsity of 95\% and recommended hyperparameters ($T=100$, $\alpha=0.3$, $T_{end}=75$% of total iterations) in the Table below.
We see that ML LinBreg is far more robust to the initialization scheme of the sparsity mask and consistently yields better or identical test accuracy to RigL.

| Method     | Mask initialization | Sparsity (%) | Test accuracy (%) |
| ---------- | ------------------- | ------------ | ----------------- |
| RigL       | Uniform             | 94.92        | 88.60             |
| RigL       | Erdős–Rényi         | 94.92        | 87.76             |
| RigL       | Erdős–Rényi–Kernel  | 94.98        | 91.27             |
| ML LinBreg | Uniform             | 94.72        | 91.42             |
| ML LinBreg | Erdős–Rényi         | 94.70        | 91.28             |
| ML LinBreg | Erdős–Rényi–Kernel  | 94.62        | 91.25             |
We will include more runs and architectures in the final paper.

Regarding the question on considerations when scaling up, we reproduced the ablation study from Figure 4 in a larger-scale setting using WideResNet28-10 on TinyImageNet. The corresponding results are shown in Figure 7 of the revised manuscript. We observe that the sparsity levels obtained with the same hyperparameters remain in a similar range as in the small-scale experiments, although they are naturally not identical.
Furthermore, the regularization parameter $\lambda$ seems to be pretty scale-invariant, and the duration of the coarse updates $m$ should be chosen slightly smaller for larger scale experiments to ensure more accurate gradient information.
